title: Sensitivity analysis for mixed binary quadratic programming
contribution: Proves that approximating the change in optimal value of an MBQP under rhs changes is NP-hard even when z(b) is known, characterises when strong duality holds between Burer's completely positive reformulation and its copositive dual (bounded P or PSD Q; counterexample otherwise; non-attainment in general) with a closed-form near-optimal dual, and turns the structure of the near-optimal dual face into an SDP method that gives tighter sensitivity dual bounds than Shor relaxations on small synthetic instances (read: arXiv v2).
problem_entry: Repeated MBQPs with a fixed constraint matrix and changing rhs; solvers find primal solutions but not matching dual bounds (App. A, p. 40); Cook et al.-type IP sensitivity bounds are trivial for binaries (p. 2).
key_idea: Use the copositive dual of Burer's CPP reformulation as a sensitivity certificate; since the epsilon-optimal dual set is never a singleton and adding KK_i blocks worsens the bound by (Delta b_i)^2, search the near-optimal dual face for a dual with small KK contribution, using an S+ + SP restriction and weights equal to the average bound over the target Delta b range (pp. 4-12).
assumptions: Assumption (A): the linear constraints imply 0<=x_j<=1 for binaries (p. 4); strong duality needs P bounded or Q PSD and a known lower bound l (p. 5); computations replace COP by S+ + SP without a guarantee (pp. 11, 36).
proof_devices: Hardness of two-sided approximation by a one-unit rhs change in an edge-colouring binary program on cubic graphs (Vizing + Holyer) (pp. 3, 16-18)
Strict copositivity of H via a recession-direction contradiction with Assumption (A) (Lemma 1, pp. 18-19)

Local stability: finite decomposition by binary patterns, an LP threshold freezing the non-empty patterns, Vavasis's QP characterisation giving a piecewise-quadratic Lipschitz lower bound (Theorem 4, pp. 19-23)
Copositivity of a closed-form dual by a three-case split of the orthant with one PSD penalty block per violated constraint type (Theorems 12-13, pp. 24-33)
Charnes-Cooper transformation to bound a linear-fractional constant (p. 26)
Counterexample min x1^2 - x2^2 with infeasible COP dual (p. 8), and non-attainment on the 6-clique stable-set COP dual by a sequence of test vectors (pp. 33-36)
experiments: Five synthetic classes (COMB, KBQP, SSLP, SSQP, PACK; n<=100) vs Shor1, Shor2, Cont; ground truth by solving each perturbed MBQP; relative gap normalised to Shor1; Julia/Gurobi/Mosek on a PC; claims the tightest bounds in all cases, but Table 1 shows 1.28 at Delta k=1 for COMB, worse than Shor1 and Cont (pp. 12-16, 40-43).
positioning: Extends IP sensitivity (Cook et al. and successors) to MBQP via Burer's CPP; credits Guo-Bodur-Taylor for CPP shadow prices and Brown et al. for part (a); parts (b)-(d) claimed new (pp. 2, 5).
writing: All results in Section 2 before the proofs; positive and negative parts in one theorem; hedged 'preliminary computations' but an unhedged 'tightest ... in all cases' (pp. 3, 5, 10, 14).
limits_future: SDP solver limits instance size; no guarantee for the S+ + SP restriction; loose constants; future: generalised copositive QCQP reformulations, scalable SDP, cutting planes using the part (b) structure (pp. 28, 36-37).

title: Regularized MIP model for integrating energy storage systems and its application for solving a trilevel interdiction problem
contribution: Adds an l1 penalty on battery charging and discharging to the DC-OPF-with-storage MIP, proves zero integrality gap with its LP relaxation above an efficiency-dependent threshold (sharp by examples), bounds the loss against the original model, and uses the regularised LP as the inner level of a trilevel battery-siting / N-k interdiction problem whose plans are certified by a relaxation-restriction sandwich (read: arXiv v2; Theorem 1 case analysis and Appendix A proofs skimmed).
problem_entry: LP relaxations of storage models allow simultaneous charging and discharging (Arroyo et al.); the exact MIP makes a trilevel N-k battery-siting problem intractable (the Zeng-An bilevel algorithm does not converge in 6 h on IEEE 14) (pp. 2, 18).
key_idea: Treat complementarity as sparsity and add an l1 regulariser; if E^min_c = E^min_d = 0 and lambda_c + eta_c eta_d lambda_d >= 1 - eta_c eta_d, the regularised MIP equals its LP relaxation, so the inner level can be dualised with bounded duals and linearised exactly (pp. 3, 6, 18, 34).
assumptions: DC OPF, identical constant battery parameters, eta_c <= 1/eta_d, zero minimum charge/discharge rates ('standard'), slack costs normalised to 1; the trilevel model drops Ohm's law and generator cost (pp. 4-5, 9, 17).
proof_devices: Exchange argument netting simultaneous charge and discharge, with a four-case objective comparison (Theorem 1, pp. 6-9)
Two-bus two-period examples showing each Theorem 1 assumption is necessary (Examples 1-2, pp. 9-10)
Degeneracy baseline: lambda >= e equals the no-battery problem (Proposition 1, p. 11)
Exactness via the gap to the second-best objective value (Proposition 2, p. 14)
Worst-case loss bound T Nb max{E^max_c lambda_c, E^max_d lambda_d} and the lambda minimising it (Theorem 3, Proposition 3, p. 15)
Sandwich z^LP <= z^OPT <= z^REG and an optimality-gap certificate for the regularised plan (Proposition 4, pp. 18-19)
Bounded third-level duals making McCormick exact (Proposition 5, p. 34)
experiments: MATPOWER IEEE/PEGASE/RTE networks with 14-1888 buses, 24-hour EIA-shaped loads with noise, Julia/Gurobi 10, 64 GB; DCOPF regularised vs exact MIP optimality gap <= 0.33% (Table 2, p. 21); trilevel solution-gap near 0 on small networks but 18-23% average on the two largest for b=5, k=10, attributed to the lower bounds (pp. 19-23).
positioning: Organises the storage-modelling literature (lossless, losses without complementarity, MIP, Pozo LP relaxations, Arroyo counterexamples); credits Singh-Knueven for the perturbation idea; places complexity between Bakhshi-Ostrowski and Bansal-Gunluk; claims the first N-k battery-siting study (pp. 2-3, 9, 24).
writing: Three bold-led contribution bullets; every theorem followed by a toy two-bus example; the conclusion's 'near-optimal solutions in most cases' is stronger than the large-network gaps (pp. 2-3, 9-16, 22, 24).
limits_future: Properties depend on the objective and constraint structure; other objectives open; NP-hardness of the lossy battery problem with fixed bounds open (p. 24); unstated: transport model in the trilevel problem, large-network plans uncertified, single-instance baseline (pp. 17-18, 22).

title: Non-monotonicity of branching rules with respect to linear relaxations
contribution: Defines monotonicity of a branching rule (a tighter relaxation never gives a larger tree), proves every fractional-only rule is non-monotonic and that one cut can blow up full-strong-branching trees exponentially, and measures prevalence on random knapsacks with cover cuts and on MIPLIB 2017 with SCIP root cuts, giving a 20%-gap-closed rule of thumb (read: arXiv v1).
problem_entry: Branch-and-cut assumes tighter formulations give smaller trees, but branching rules use local LP information; made precise after removing dual degeneracy and fixing best-bound node selection (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: Explicit small polytopes where the tighter formulation makes a variable integral at all vertices (so a fractional-only rule loses a good split), and a 2-D gadget replicated n times and coupled through one auxiliary variable so that a single cut tightens all copies and flips FSB's choices (pp. 3-8).
assumptions: Integer programs with nested LP relaxations having the same integer points; non-degenerate objectives; best-bound node selection; FSB with product, linear (mu = 1/6) or ratio score (pp. 2-3).
proof_devices: 4-D polytope from three vertex sets related to the cross-polytope; the tighter Q is the lift-and-project closure of P in x4; trees of 11 vs 15 nodes (Theorem 1, pp. 4-5)
2-D gadget with a vertex table and hand-computed FSB-P scores (Table 1, pp. 6-7)
n copies coupled by an auxiliary variable in a redundant constraint so that one cut acts as n cuts (pp. 6-7)
Upper bound by the recursion T(n) <= 4 + T(n-1); lower bound by counting complete gadgets before pruning by bound, >= 6(2^floor(0.75n/6.75) - 1) (pp. 7-8)
Monotone extremes (a-priori order; #P-hard optimal branching) bounding the open question (p. 13)
experiments: 100 random MKPs (n=20, m=50) with exact cover separation in a Python naive B&B with FSB as an oracle (19.8% of single cuts enlarge trees; weak correlation with gap closed and depth); 21 filtered MIPLIB 2017 instances in stripped SCIP 8 with the optimal value supplied, 3 seeds, 0-10 cut rounds; no tree growth beyond 20% gap closed (pp. 8-12).
positioning: Places itself in branch-and-cut history and recent branching-vs-cutting trade-off studies (Basu et al.; Kazachkov-Le Bodic-Sankaranarayanan); builds on his own FSB, random-IP and cut-selection papers; uses the Gamrath-Schubert fair node-counting protocol (pp. 1, 9, 13).
writing: Formal definition before results; the insight sentence repeated in abstract, contributions and experiments; 'Contrary to expectation', 'surprisingly common'; the conclusion guards against over-reading and disclaims evaluating SCIP (pp. 2-3, 9, 11-13).
limits_future: Dual degeneracy uncontrolled in MIPLIB and confounding the zero-gap instances; open whether a good, efficient, monotone rule exists; unstated: small instance sets, only FSB-P, threshold read from scatter plots (pp. 10, 12-13).

quotes.text: Contrary to expectation, 19.8% of the cuts led to an increase in tree size.

Through this work, we show that such aberrant behaviour may not always be because of engineering reasons like the addition of cuts leading to a change in some default parameters or other random tie-breaking, but the problem may in fact be mathematical in nature.
